whatItFakes: P15 kin and temperament generation coefficients (relative proximity, birth spacing, first-birth spread, paternal age gap, men's fertility lag, upbringing shift, facet correlations, reference age) are prototype values.
why: Families and temperaments must be generated now; no instrument-matched source fixes these coefficients yet.
replacement: Coefficients sourced from NSFG, natality and NEO-PI-R facet tables and checked against the P15 answer keys.

whatItFakes: Kin outside the household are generated per resident household as husk-tier people: every relative alive or not by the SSA cohort life table for their birth year (Actuarial Study No. 120, birth decades 1900-2010 interpolated), siblings by size-biased cohort fertility, children and grandchildren by Census children ever born; relatives are never matched to other residents, partners of siblings and adult children and cousins are absent, and residence is only county or state, set by whether each adult moved away (state ACS leaving rates times a tunable share) and whether the parents' marriage held (NSFG).
why: Every resident needs real family consistent with age; a full kin-matching and migration engine does not exist.
replacement: Researched Oct 24, 2026: how near relatives live is in data/research/people/pew-parent-proximity-2005.json (Pew 2006: 65% of adults with a living parent live within an hour's drive of that parent) and data/research/people/pew-extended-family-proximity-2021.json (Pew 2022: 55% near at least some extended family, by Census region, with a table for all 56 places), reported against the town by scripts/research/people-year.ts; the builder item people-kin-placement-by-distance places and matches relatives by them. A kin engine that matches relatives to residents across households and places, with partners, cousins and observed migration distances.

whatItFakes: The five temperament dimensions are read from five NEO facets (CTO-approved October 10, 2026) with BLSA age curves, IPIP-NEO sex differences and NEO-PI-R manual facet correlations; each dimension uses one facet rather than its own norms.
why: The owner's five dimensions have no published norms of their own; facet norms are the nearest sourced spread.
replacement: Researched Oct 24, 2026: the A4 quadratic term is zero by the source itself. Terracciano and others (2005) Table 2, read at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2808690/, fits A4 Compliance as a straight line ("The quadratic terms are presented only when the quadratic model fit the data better than the linear model"). Every facet's curve in opening-kin.json and the two facet correlations (psychTools 2.6.4 dataset neo, read from the package data) are checked by scripts/research/people-parameters-check.ts against data/research/people/terracciano-blsa-neo-facets-2005.json and data/research/people/neo-pi-r-facet-correlations-1992.json. Still open, so personalitySociabilityRiskCorrelation and personalityReliabilityImpulseCorrelation stay ESTIMATED: norms measured on the five dimensions themselves, which would make both correlations SOURCED.

whatItFakes: Closeness is hours together over hours plus a sourced half-closeness point, fading by a tunable half-life; opening closeness uses the average GSS visit rate for the tie and a registered conversion of answer categories to visits, not each pair's history.
why: No survey measures closeness in hours or its decay without contact; Hall (2019) gives hour thresholds and Roberts and Dunbar (2015) only the direction of decay.
replacement: Closeness calibrated against a panel of measured tie strength and contact (for example, the Roberts and Dunbar network data or a US panel), with per-pair opening histories from the shared past. Researched Oct 23, 2026 (research-core-sourced-parameters): Roberts and Dunbar (Human Nature, 2015) slopes, kin +0.27 and friends -0.62 points a wave on a 1 to 10 scale, and inner-layer retention over 18 months (kin 70.3%, friends 48.6%), with Hall's hours to friendship (KU News, 2018), are in data/research/core/tie-decay-panels-2015.json; scripts/research/core-year.ts reports a town's yearly closeness change by tie kind against them. Still open: no source read gives a half-life of closeness without contact or a pair's own opening history; the builder item core-stopgap-closeness-relationship-closeness-model reads the file.

whatItFakes: Opening household members are aged from the place's records by household type: the chance of having a partner now comes from a yearly chain of first marriage (ACS 2024 never-married shares by age), divorce (NSFG women's first-marriage survival, used for every marriage), widowhood (SSA 2023 life table, with the spouse's age from the CPS 2023 spouse age gap) and remarriage (NCFMR 2022); a partner's age follows the national CPS 2023 spouse age gap for every couple, including same-sex couples; parents of children under 18 follow national CPS 2023 parents by age and living arrangement; a household of related housemates is always one parent and one grown child; parents' grown children at home are a seeded count from the parent's births and the place's share of adults living in a parent's home (ACS B09021); homes of unrelated housemates take the place's nonfamily household sizes (B11016), each housemate's sex and age drawn on their own. Cohabitation is not a separate path, places outside the ACS 1-year survey read their state, and four territories read the nation (ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE).
why: No source gives each opening adult's partnership history or household; the chain and the CPS tables turn sourced rates into ages by sex and household type. Partnered adults keep the household generator's sex; people living alone and housemates draw sex with age.
replacement: Place-level ACS 5-year sex-by-age, marital-status and household-relationship tables for every seated place and territory, cohabitation and second-marriage survival from NSFG, the spouse age gap and parents' ages by place, and siblings, grandparents raising grandchildren and older parents living in a grown child's home seated as their own household types. Oct 23, 2026 (research-deep-past-sourced-parameters): spouseAgeGapOpenRowYears re-estimated from the CPS 2023 ASEC public use file (U.S. Census Bureau, 2023; ESTIMATED, 16 years, spread 14 to 22), read by opening-partnership.ts SPOUSE_GAP; it becomes SOURCED when the engine reads the measured single-year tail in place of an even spread. data/research/core/cps-asec-2023-partner-age-gap.json also holds the measured gap bands of same-sex married couples and of opposite- and same-sex cohabiting couples for the builder item art-stopgap-opening-partnership-estimated-behavior; place-level tables and the four territories remain open, and their rows already wait unread on main in data/research/stopgaps-oct19/census/census-SG-P15-partnership-model.json (2020 Island Areas census rows for the four territories) and census-SG-P15-partnership-model-places.json (place rows).

whatItFakes: How far a relative lives changes how often they are visited only by whether they are in the household's county (full pull) or elsewhere in the state (0.39 of it, from Pew 2005 daily contact by same or different town).
why: Relatives outside the town carry only a county or state, not a place, so no travel distance exists to read.
replacement: Travel time between the two people's places once relatives carry a place, from the Census Gazetteer interior points the repository already holds (data/source/places/corpus.json, data/source/counties/corpus.json), with visits falling with travel time; builder item core-kin-visits-by-distance. Until then farKinContactShare is ESTIMATED at 0.39 (spread 0.39 to 0.49) from Pew Research Center 2006, contact with a parent in town against out of town (data/research/core/pew-2006-family-contact.json, checked by scripts/research/core-parameters-check.ts). The measured figure that would make it SOURCED is a U.S. table of contact by travel time: none was found on Oct 23, 2026, and the French INED table a search named was not reachable from the cloud session.

whatItFakes: Each child's school is a seeded pick among the public schools teaching their entry grade in their place, else in their county and its places, else (for places the county geography does not cover: the territories and Puerto Rico) in their state or territory, weighted by students per grade and shared by children who live together. Attendance boundaries, chosen public schools (19% of students in NCES 2016), private schools and homeschooling are not modeled; the 2023-24 directory stands in for earlier decades; the 815 schools without a reported grade span (all 28 in American Samoa) are left out, so American Samoa keeps generated school names.
why: No attendance boundary or historical school directory is in the repository; P12 supplies each public school's place, grades and enrollment.
replacement: NCES EDGE school attendance boundaries (SABS) with the household's location, private school (PSS) and homeschool shares by state, and historical CCD directories for each cohort's years.

whatItFakes: An employer's full staff is split into workgroups of about openingCoworkerGroupSize by the world's seed (who knows whom, never what anyone does), and each person meets their workgroup on the opening day through the encounters engine (meetAtWork). Two jobs at one employer count as shared work without checking that their spans overlap, because a job record keeps no start date. Departments, shifts and coworkers outside the town are not modeled. Oct 28, 2026 (wire-people-and-director, engine map line 12): the generated social:generated-coworker facts and their writer are deleted; the workgroup is read from the jobs engine's staff list.
why: Employers carry no departments or teams, and no source gives how many coworkers a person knows.
replacement: Workgroups from occupation and establishment records (BLS OEWS staffing patterns by industry) and a measured number of coworkers known, with time worked together adding to closeness on the shifts both attend.

whatItFakes: Grief starts at the closeness to the person who died and halves every personal half-life; the half-life spread is solved from two Bonanno et al. (2002) pattern shares with 'little grief' set at a quarter of the starting grief (TUNABLE). Grief pulls toward rest and contact with family and holds back organizing with tunable weights. Losses are kept in memory, not in a save.
why: Owner's ruling, October 10, 2026 (CTO on #3942): a personal resilience line, calibrated to about 46% with little grief by 6 months and 15.6% still grieving at 18 months; P10 reported a widow organizing on the day her husband died.
replacement: A grief measure matched to a bereavement instrument (for example the grief items Bonanno et al. used), choice weights checked against observed behavior after a loss, and losses saved with the world.

whatItFakes: Falling-outs in the shared past build from the years a pair shared a class or workgroup and both people's conflict and reliability traits, with tunable trait weights; the base rate is solved to YouGov's lifetime share of adults who ended a friendship, which counts all friendships, not only classmates and coworkers. Favors are not generated: no dated recorded need (a move, a job loss, an illness) exists in the shared past.
why: CTO, October 10, 2026 (#3938): generate favors and falling-outs in the shared past so the director can bring a person back with stakes. Resolved Oct 16, 2026 (core-standins-opening-deletions): deleted. Nothing read the falling-out facts (no engine or director line used them), so they were a record with no read; the two-level rule gives nobody a full past before they are filled in. The generator, its data and its three parameters are gone.
replacement: A friendship-ending rate among classmates and coworkers by years known, temperament weights checked against a study of conflict and personality, and favors from dated recorded needs.

whatItFakes: A person's free hours are filled from one scoring pass per activation: at most one act per need each day, and every act after the activation's own pick must score above zero. Between planned days, needs other than company are held at their activation value and lowered only by the planned acts' own effects; the plan lives in memory, not in a save, and the ATUS caregiving time per participant-day stands for one act of care.
why: The CTO's part 2b decision (October 10, 2026): one scoring pass per free block for daily-tier people and a week planned forward for weekly-tier people, within 20% of part 2's speed.
replacement: A complete daily time budget that reserves the ATUS time of activities the game does not model, needs that evolve on each planned day from their own causes, and plans saved with the world. Researched Oct 23, 2026 (research-core-sourced-parameters): the ATUS time of unmodeled activities is already reserved (src/core2/data/free-block.json, BLS ATUS 2025 Table 3); the visit band is ATUS 2025 Table 1 socializing and communicating (30.4% of people a day, men 28.2%, women 32.5%) in data/research/core/atus-2025-socializing.json, reported by scripts/research/core-year.ts. unmodeledLeisureValuePerHour stays TUNABLE: no published effect converts to its score units. Still open: one act per need a day, needs held between planned days and plans kept out of the save; the builder item core-free-block-daily-budget.

whatItFakes: Favors in the shared past come only at a resident's recorded move into the county, from people they shared a class or workgroup with, by closeness at the time from a tunable hours-per-shared-year; the rate is solved to an opt-in commercial poll (39% first ask friends for help moving). Residents' birthplaces are all their own town, so an adult move reads as moving back; job losses and illness come in part 5's lived years.
why: CTO, October 10, 2026, 8:12 p.m. (#3938): generate dated moves first, then favors from close classmates or coworkers at the time of a move. Resolved Oct 16, 2026 (core-standins-opening-deletions): deleted with the falling-outs. No engine read a favor fact; recorded moves keep their own facts, and a favor between two people would come from a dated need in play, not a generated past.
replacement: A probability-sample source on help received at a move, closeness at the time from a measured friendship model, out-of-town birthplaces from ACS place of birth, and favors at job losses and illness.

whatItFakes: New people are met only on a visit (the host's household) and on joining a group (its other members); the first tie holds the act's hours. Meetings at an organized meeting wait for attendance, and new coworkers for jobs changing during play (M1).
why: Owner's ruling, October 10, 2026 (CTO on #3956): build encounters 1 and 2 now, 3 with M1's jobs work.
replacement: Encounters at meetings with attendance, new coworkers when jobs change, neighbors once addresses exist, and first-tie hours checked against a study of how acquaintances form.

whatItFakes: Relatives living outside the town (husk-tier kin) are not run through the years before the start: they keep only their family and move facts, with no school years or working life.
why: They never act, and generating that history for every relative made the prepared town too large to serialize (La Homa: 861 MB of past facts with part 1).
replacement: Run a relative's years before the start when the game first simulates them (the school engine's later hook, src/core2/past-school.ts schoolHistoryFor, and the working life's pastWorkFor).

whatItFakes: Opening views read the person's state and age band (the CES cell), their education and faith profile (opening-profile.ts, itself a stopgap) and a household heritage; the 14 values and issue stances at the opening are not formed. Stances move only on events with a topic and on speeches.
why: First version of views on the new core, built while the people records gain education and faith.
replacement: Researched Oct 24, 2026: the place-type term is in data/research/people/pew-partisanship-community-type-2023.json (Pew Research Center 2024, registered voters: urban counties 60% Democratic and 37% Republican, suburban 47% and 50%, rural a 25-point Republican edge), reported beside the town's opening lean by scripts/research/people-year.ts; education and faith already come from the CES 2024 keys and the stance loadings. The 14 values have no answer key yet. Builder item people-views-opening-place-type-and-values. Opening views from the person's education, faith, place type and upbringing through CES-derived weights; the 14 values; conversations and news moving stances (M1-10, M2-09).

whatItFakes: How much each recorded reason weighs in deciding to run for office, and the pull of staying out.
why: The research names the reasons (interest, a personal stake, temperament, money, time, age) but not their sizes in this model.
replacement: Weights checked against candidate counts per seat across drawn places once GOV's contests run every cycle (M2-04).

whatItFakes: How fast outlets reach people by how closely they follow politics, how long a story stays news, and how many stories pass at a contact; one generic local outlet stands for all.
why: Basic news (M2-09) needs a first version before outlets and media habits are modeled.
replacement: Named local outlets with real audiences and each person's recorded media habits (Pew local news surveys), checked against how fast election results spread. Oct 23, 2026 (research-gov-sourced-parameters): newsOutletDelayDays is ESTIMATED at 1 day (spread 1 to 2) from The Media Insight Project's 2014 news-frequency split and Pew's 2022 share who follow the news most of the time (data/research/news/apnorc-2014-news-frequency.json, data/research/news/pew-2024-2025-news-habits.json), read by scheduleDeliveries in src/core2/modules/news.ts and heardOn in src/core2/past-news.ts; it becomes SOURCED with a measured delay from print to reading by how closely people follow the news. newsMaxAgeDays is read as a cutoff, so it is not sourced: people-news-newsMaxAgeDays-as-cause. newsStoriesPerContact has no convertible source; the share of adults word of mouth reaches is checked against Pew's 2025 Local News Fact Sheet by scripts/research/gov-year.ts.

whatItFakes: How much a speech moves listeners and who retells it; retelling reaches only the listener's household.
why: Speeches (M4-04) need a first reception model; persuasion research gives directions and small averages, not these coefficients.
replacement: Reception calibrated to persuasion experiments by audience and message, retelling through friends and the news module, and memory by age (M4-04). Researched Oct 23, 2026: Coppock, Hill and Vavreck 2020 (Science Advances 6(36):eabc4046) measure 0.049 points on a 1 to 5 favorability scale per advertisement (SD 0.07 across 59 experiments), held as a band of 0.012 (0 to 0.030) stance strength per message in data/research/core/coppock-2020-ad-persuasion.json and reported against by scripts/research/core-parameters-year.ts. No published effect converts to speechImpulse or speechRetellWeight, so they stay TUNABLE. Oct 25, 2026 (traits-retell-circumstances): speechKeepPull and the two engagement weights of the retelling case are ESTIMATED from ANES 2020 talk at home by interest, and the retelling weighs who is at home to hear it.

whatItFakes: How much traits, money pressure and ties weigh in offering, taking and telling about a bribe.
why: Basic corruption (M3-09) needs a first version; the research gives directions, not these coefficients.
replacement: Weights checked against bribery incidence surveys and public-corruption case counts by office (DOJ Public Integrity Section reports, data/research/corruption/roadmap-r29-aggregate-enforcement.json), with audits and the news surfacing records; the take calibration is people-corruption-honest-pull-calibrated. Researched Oct 23, 2026 (data/research/core/corruption-bands-2014.json): bribes averaged 10.9% of a deal's value and 34.5% of its profit in 427 OECD foreign-bribery cases (OECD Foreign Bribery Report 2014, via a secondary summary; the OECD pages refused the session), the figure bribeShareOfStake would take as ESTIMATED, and 7% of U.S. adults paid a bribe to a public service in a year (Transparency International, Global Corruption Barometer 2013, via Pew Research Center), the band scripts/research/core-parameters-year.ts reports offers against. The trait, need, tie, tell, quiet, report, vote and breach weights have no published effect that converts and stay TUNABLE.

whatItFakes: How often a taken bribe leads to a telling and a press tip in one played year: officials keep a median-or-better cushion, so a town takes a handful of bribes a year at the Pletzer-calibrated take pull, and a falling-out (an award that went to another firm, a bill voted the other way) between the two parties needs one of those few to be cheated before corruption.tell and press.tip are weighed.
why: Takes now fire (seated officials' savings spread around the SCF median, officialSavingsSpreadSigma) and contract awards settle a taken bribe (settleBribe), but in the audited years the bought firm won every award, so no tie soured and no one was told. Forcing a breach would be a dice-free but invented mechanic.
replacement: Measure the share of taken bribes cheated across 56 drawn places over several years (scripts/research/core-parameters-year.ts) and calibrate the official savings spread and the bribe-share-of-stake against Global Corruption Barometer incidence; or let a letdown arise from the contract engine's own losing bidders.

whatItFakes: Each adult's education and faith at the opening, read from their state's CES 2024 shares by age band with a household share; education and faith are treated as independent within a state and age band, and children carry no attainment.
why: Views and candidacy need education and faith on records now; joint state tables are too sparse in one survey year.
replacement: Attainment from the person's own schooling history (deep past) checked against ACS B15001 by state, age and sex; faith from upbringing and the Pew Religious Landscape Study. Oct 23, 2026 (research-deep-past-sourced-parameters): the check tables are in data/research/core/acs-2023-b15001-attainment-by-state.json (ACS 2019-2023 B15001 by state, age and sex) and data/research/core/pew-rls-2023-24-faith-by-state.json (Pew Research Center Religious Landscape Study 2023-24, by state), both for all 56 places, reported against the opening profile by scripts/research/deep-past-year.ts. The builder item core-opening-profile-attainment-from-schooling derives attainment and faith from the person's own record and checks the town against them.

whatItFakes: How strongly each tie holds a person in town and each event pushes them out, and the scale that turns the ACS rate for their age into a monthly pull.
why: The research gives how often people of each age leave a county and the reasons movers give, but not each tie's and event's size in this model.
replacement: Weights checked against ACS departures by age and tenure across drawn places in the M1-09 year run, and against the CPS reasons for moving. Oct 23, 2026: the owner and job holds are ESTIMATED as log ratios of CPS ASEC 2023 different-county move rates (data/research/core/cps-asec-2023-mobility.json). The children and kin holds convert to 0.32 (CPS ASEC 2023 Table 6) and 0.30 per relative (Spring, Ackert, Crowder and South 2017, data/research/core/spring-2017-kin-proximity.json) but stay at their starting values, 0.4 and 0.15, with the converted figures as their spreads, because applying them takes src/core2/moves.test.ts past its departure band while the engine already sends about 1.75 times the expected adults away; world-town-net-moving-negative applies them once the departure rate is right. All are checked by scripts/research/core-parameters-check.ts; the figures that would make them SOURCED are effects net of age. The cutoff and caps are gone: who decides alone is the place's age of majority (data/research/people/age-of-majority.json), kin hold and pull slide with movesKinHoldDecay, and the housing push rises with the share of the household's income and net cash its home takes. The other pulls and pushes stay TUNABLE: scripts/research/core-parameters-year.ts reports a town's departures against the ACS 2024 rate for its adults and the share of leavers by recorded cause against the CPS different-county reasons.

whatItFakes: A person who moved away keeps their town place and household on their record; the inactive tier and the departure record say they left.
why: The core has no call to change a person's place or household mid-run.
replacement: A core call (OPUS-CORE) that moves a person to the destination place and out of their household, so counts, voter rolls and screens read the new place. Done Oct 13 (FIXER-MOVES): the core's relocatePeopleV1 moves leavers to the destination place and county, and out of their household (whole households move with them), so counts, voter rolls and screens read the new place.

whatItFakes: A household that owns its home with a mortgage and has members who stay in town does not leave together; only a grown child in it can move out. A household that leaves entirely sells its home, pays off its mortgage and takes the surplus.
why: Splitting a mortgaged home between those who go and those who stay (who keeps the home and the loan) is not modeled.
replacement: A recorded decision of who keeps a home and its mortgage when some of a household's members leave, so that groups can leave with part of the household behind.

whatItFakes: No one in the player's own household moves away through the engine, so the player is never left alone with a lease, no job and no cash when the adults who earn leave town.
why: Fraser, Colorado (seed d8c9a58e, place 0828305): at 17 the player's parents and siblings moved away on Feb 12 with their cash and the household's only job, and the player's lease went into arrears and ended. Whether parents may leave an 18-year-old player behind, and with what, is the owner's call; no ruling exists in the decision register.
replacement: Background households may split from an 18-year-old when cheap to simulate and as common as in real life, but the player's own family does not leave the player before 1.0, so the hold in moves.ts stays.

whatItFakes: A person whose job a saved agreement names as its provider's qualification (a visitor's lodging, a public supplier contract) does not move away; moves keeps its own copy of the jobs engine's lookup of those jobs.
why: The core rejects such an agreement's next payment once the job ends, and the jobs engine's lookup is not exported.
replacement: Agreements re-resolve their qualifying worker when a job ends (WORLD/CORE), and the jobs engine exports its pinned-job lookup; then these holders can move like anyone else. Resolved by Same change, October 19, 2026: the moves engine's copy of the lookup is deleted, so a holder of a job a saved agreement names moves like anyone else and the agreement re-resolves at its next payment (finance-cash.ts productJobRelations).

whatItFakes: A party's asks for a seat stop at the player: when the player says no or not now in the ask's scene, the party asks none of its other members for that seat.
why: The party asks on the day filing opens, and the player's answer comes later, from the scene; nothing returns the party to its list once the player has answered.
replacement: The candidacy engine reads the player's no or not-now reply (a scene.reply naming the party-asked record) and asks the party's next member for the seat while filing is open.

whatItFakes: The order a party's chair asks its members to run: those the chair is closest to first, then those the most people know. A new 18-year-old member is rarely first unless they are close to the chair or the party has few members.
why: Decided by the owner's rulings, not a question: "The party asks someone to run only with some inroads on record" (OWNER-DECISIONS, Oct 15, night, batch 13 review) and "a player with a high-standing job may be propositioned to run for a seat someone needs filled" (OWNER-DECISIONS, Oct 14, CTO from standing rules); recorded as an acting-lead ruling, Oct 26. Read: OWNER-DECISIONS (Oct 26, evening), DECISION-REGISTER, prior-rulings/elections.md and prior-rulings/words.md, LAW; searched: party asks, propositioned, recruit, Pendergast.
replacement: Resolved: the chair asks members with inroads first (closeness to the chair), then those the most people know (standing), per the rulings quoted in why.
